demos.title: Why is the Arctic warming fastest?

steps.caption: Start in the Arctic Ocean north of Siberia. The deep red tells us this spot has warmed faster than almost anywhere else since 1981. Scientists call this Arctic amplification.
Slide back to 1990 and the colours almost vanish. Only nine years of change had built up by then, so the globe is nearly neutral.
Now jump to 2040. The dotted line continues the trend, and the screen edges glow orange to remind you this is a projection, not a measurement.
Compare with the tropical Pacific. The change here is smaller and the colours softer, even though it is the same variable and the same 45 years.

demos.title: Is the Sahel getting wetter again?

steps.caption: The Sahel is the strip of grassland south of the Sahara. After terrible droughts in the 1970s and 80s, rainfall here has partly recovered since 1981.
Look at the graph in the panel. The thin line jumps around every year, which is why one wet or dry year never proves a trend. The trend line and its shaded band are what matter.
Fly north to the Mediterranean, between Italy and Greece, and the sign flips to blue: rain here is slowly falling. Rain is moving around the planet, not just going up or down everywhere.

demos.title: Where did the haze go, and where did it come from?

steps.caption: Over the Indo-Gangetic Plain, aerosol optical depth, a measure of how hazy the air is, has risen strongly since 2001, when this record begins, as cities and industry grew.
Western Europe shows the opposite. Clean-air laws cut sulphur and smoke, and the air has kept getting clearer since 2001. Blue here is good news.
Switch to sunlight at the same spot. Clearer air lets more of the sun's energy reach the ground, a phenomenon called brightening. Two variables, one story.
Antarctica is where the ozone hole appears every spring. Ozone is measured in Dobson units: the thickness the layer would have if squashed down to the ground.
The badge tells you whether the change is real or could be random. Ozone swings a lot from year to year, so even large changes can fail the significance test.
The projection simply extends the straight line. Real ozone recovery depends on the Montreal Protocol and chemistry, so treat this line as a question, not an answer.
Pale, see-through areas are places where the trend is not statistically significant. The numbers still show a slope, but it is small compared with the year-to-year noise.
Open the Numbers section. A p-value above 0.05 means that if nothing were really changing, we would still see a slope this big more than one time in twenty.
Fly to Southeast Asia. Warmer air holds more water vapour, so humidity here has risen clearly, and the colour is strong rather than pale.
